title: Living as if No One Is Watching
overview: This psalm describes people who live as though God does not exist, how they prey on the vulnerable, and a longing for God to step in and set things right.

parts.label: The fool's claim (v. 1)
parts.note: The Hebrew word for fool here means someone morally reckless, not unintelligent, and "there is no God" is less an argument than a private wish that no one will ever hold them to account. Living by that idea, the psalm says, produces rotten and shameful behavior.

parts.label: God looks down (vv. 2-3)
parts.note: God is pictured searching all humanity for anyone who understands and seeks him, and finding that everyone has turned aside and gone bad, like something spoiled. Christians read these lines through the apostle Paul, who quotes them in his letter to the Romans to argue that every person falls short and needs God's grace.

parts.label: Those who devour the poor (vv. 4-6)
parts.note: These evildoers consume ordinary people as casually as eating a meal and never pray, which suggests they don't care about God more than that they don't know him. Yet the psalm pictures them overwhelmed with dread right where they stand, because God is present with the people they crush and shelters the poor whose plans they spoil.

parts.label: A longing for rescue (v. 7)
parts.note: Zion means Jerusalem, seen as the place where God dwelt, and the psalmist longs for rescue to come from there. The phrase about God restoring his people can mean bringing captives home or reversing misfortune more generally, and scholars are unsure whether it points to a specific event such as the return from exile in Babylon.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether "there is no one who does good" describes every human being's corrupted nature, as many read it following Paul, or mainly describes the oppressors in this psalm, set against the righteous poor whom God protects.
think: When people act as if no one will ever hold them to account, what do you think changes in how they treat those weaker than themselves?
